content: The target population and the realities on the ground must be carefully considered, particularly in relation to the availability of local resources such as human resources, cold chain equipment, transportation, waste management systems, per-diem payments for health workers, and the involvement of community leaders. Collaboration with other ministries, such as the Ministry of Education, as well as NGOs and faith-based organizations, is essential to ensure the success of supplementary immunization activities (SIAs) for measles and rubella. Key characteristics of successful measles-rubella SIAs include their integration into broader disease control or elimination frameworks, strong country ownership, political commitment from leaders and stakeholders, bottom-up planning, active community participation, and meticulous micro-planning to prevent supply disruptions. Effective monitoring and documentation are critical, with administrative coverage exceeding 95% in all districts and minimal pockets of unvaccinated children, especially in hard-to-reach areas. National-level administrative coverage must be validated through coverage surveys, and inputs such as vaccines, devices, and human resources should be used efficiently with minimal wastage. Adverse events following immunization (AEFIs) must be closely monitored and managed. Partnerships with local organizations should be strengthened, and immunization waste disposal must be conducted safely to avoid harm to health workers or the community. Macro-level planning at the national level is vital to secure political commitment, develop realistic budgets, mobilize resources, and ensure timely procurement of vaccines, cold chain equipment, and related supplies. This planning process should include a thorough review of past performance to identify and reinforce successful local practices. Engaging faith-based organizations, civil society groups, and other stakeholders during the planning stage can help pool resources that may otherwise be inaccessible. Special attention should be given to addressing barriers that prevent underserved populations from being reached. The micro-plan should specify the required quantities of vaccines, auto-disable syringes, reconstitution syringes, and safety boxes, ensuring accurate estimation of the target population. All items must be ordered at least six months before the SIA dates to allow for vaccine production, shipment, clearance at ports, and inland distribution. Vaccination teams must be carefully composed and adequately trained to ensure the success of mass campaigns. These teams typically consist of vaccinators and volunteers. Vaccinators, who are trained health workers, are responsible for vaccine reconstitution, administration, safe waste disposal, responding to adverse events, summarizing and reporting vaccination data, and supervising volunteers. Volunteers assist with crowd control, screening children, recording and tallying data, mobilizing the community, and identifying unvaccinated children. The number of children vaccinated per team per day can vary depending on population density, with rural and sparsely populated areas presenting unique challenges. Bottom-up micro-planning allows for these ground realities to be recognized and addressed. Injection safety and waste disposal protocols must be strictly followed during SIAs. Needles should not be recapped, and used syringes and needles must be discarded in safety boxes. At the end of each day, safety boxes should be transported to designated health facilities for incineration. If incinerators are unavailable, plans should be made to store the safety boxes for later centralized incineration. Other waste should be disposed of in bins and incinerated alongside the safety boxes. Given the large quantities of waste generated during SIAs, special measures must be planned, including inventories of functioning incinerators, transportation logistics, and incineration capacity assessments. To prevent adverse events following immunization (AEFIs), the micro-plan must outline measures to avoid programmatic errors and ensure proper AEFI management. Health worker training is critical, as is the provision of adequate supplies, including diluents and AEFI management kits. Vaccinators must be trained in the use of these kits, and AEFI committees must be functional during the campaign. A crisis communication plan should be developed and disseminated to manage public concerns in the event of a serious AEFI. Intensive supervision is necessary to ensure the quality of SIA implementation. Supervisors at all levels should guide and support personnel, receiving refresher training to enhance their skills and activities. An effective monitoring system must be established to measure campaign quality and address gaps before the campaign concludes. Real-time coverage data should be collected at all levels, enabling rapid transmission to control rooms at intermediate and national levels. Tally sheets must be carefully designed to collect essential information without being overly complex. Monitoring campaign quality at the local level during SIAs is intended to address operational issues that may hinder universal coverage. Unvaccinated individuals identified during monitoring should either be vaccinated on-site or directed to the nearest immunization site. In areas with several unvaccinated individuals, vaccination teams should be redeployed to ensure comprehensive coverage. This requires flexibility in tactical operations, including team management and resource allocation. Local-level SIA campaign quality monitoring is often conducted through rapid coverage monitoring (RCM), which focuses on high-risk populations and convenience samples. However, RCM is not a scientifically valid method for generalizing overall campaign coverage. Post-campaign assessments, such as lot quality assurance sampling (LQAS) or coverage surveys, provide more representative data. LQAS results in binary classifications (pass or fail) for specific lots, while coverage surveys offer quantitative estimates with confidence intervals. These assessments help identify areas with inadequate coverage, validate administrative data, and determine reasons for missed vaccinations to improve follow-up efforts.
